title: Demonstrate an understanding of soil preparation

lessons.title: Why we prepare soil
lessons.html:
Why we prepare soil

Before a crop or orchard or vineyard is planted, the soil must be made ready. Good soil preparation gives roots space to grow, lets water soak in and drain away, and gives the plants the food (nutrients) they need. Mistakes made now are hard to fix later, especially for vines and fruit trees that stay for many years.

Steps in soil preparation

  1. Soil sampling and testing. Samples are taken and sent to a laboratory. The results show if the soil is too acid (low pH), which nutrients are missing, and if there are hard layers. The farm manager or adviser then decides what to add.
  2. Clearing the land. Remove old plants, roots, stumps, stones and rubbish. Old vine or tree roots should be removed because they can carry diseases and nematodes.
  3. Deep loosening (ripping). A tractor pulls a ripper or deep plough to break hard layers deep in the soil, so roots and water can go down.
  4. Adding lime and fertiliser. Lime makes acid soil less acid. Phosphorus and other nutrients may also be worked in deep, because they do not move down easily later.
  5. Levelling and shaping. The land may be smoothed, and ridges or contour banks may be made so water does not wash the soil away.
  6. Final cultivation. The top soil is worked to a fine, even layer ready for planting.

Timing

Soil preparation for perennial crops such as vines often starts months before planting. Ripping works best when the soil is dry enough to crack and shatter. Working very wet soil damages it and makes hard clods.

Your supervisor will tell you which steps your farm uses and when. Each farm and soil is different.

lessons.title: Working safely and protecting the soil
lessons.html:
Working safely and protecting the soil

Your jobs during soil preparation

  • Taking soil samples as you are shown.
  • Picking up stones, roots and old wire.
  • Spreading lime or compost by hand or helping with the spreader.
  • Marking lines and pegs.
  • Helping the tractor driver by checking the depth and watching for obstacles.

How to take a soil sample

  1. Use a clean spade or soil auger and a clean bucket.
  2. Walk across the block in a zig-zag and take small amounts of soil from many spots.
  3. Take each sample at the depth your supervisor gives, for example topsoil and subsoil kept separately.
  4. Do not sample near kraals, fertiliser heaps, roads or old fences; these spots are not normal.
  5. Mix the soil, fill the sample bag and label it with the block name, depth and date.

Protecting the soil

Soil is a natural resource that takes a very long time to form. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 requires farmers to protect soil from erosion.

  • Work across the slope, not up and down.
  • Do not leave bare soil for long periods; plant a cover crop if there is a delay.
  • Keep machines off very wet soil to avoid compaction.
  • Keep contour banks and water channels in good repair.

Safety

  • Stay well away from tractors and implements when they are working. Never ride on a ripper or plough.
  • Make eye contact with the driver before you go near a machine. Only approach when it has stopped.
  • Wear a dust mask and gloves when spreading lime or fertiliser, and wash afterwards.
  • Lift bags with bent knees; get help with heavy bags.
  • Drink water and wear a hat; land preparation is hot, dusty work.

Key points

  • Good soil preparation lets roots grow and water soak in and drain.
  • Test the soil first, so lime and fertiliser are correct.
  • Clear old roots, rip hard layers, add lime, shape the land and cultivate.
  • Take soil samples from many spots in a zig-zag and label them.
  • Protect soil from erosion and never go near working machines.
